newsitem.title: USA: Union Pacific seeks to acquire Pennzoil for $6.4 billion.
newsitem.headline: Union Pacific seeks to acquire Pennzoil for $6.4 billion.

text.p: Union Pacific Resources Group Inc. Monday offered to buy Pennzoil Co. in a two-step deal worth about $3.9 billion, stepping up the pressure on the independent oil producer after on-again, off-again merger talks.
Including assumption of debt, the deal would be worth about $6.4 billion.
News of the offer, valued at $84 per Pennzoil share, sent the stock soaring, and it was up $17.875 at $77.50 on the New York Stock Exchange.

Pennzoil management said it would review the offer and promised a response on or before July 7. It asked Pennzoil shareholders to defer taking any action on the Union Pacific tender offer until the company issues its response.
"We believe that the merger of UPR and Pennzoil will create the premier independent exploration and production company in the U.S.," Union Pacific Resources Chairman Jack Messman said in a statement.

"Driven by UPR's proven ability to drill and develop oil and gas properties quickly and efficiently, we are confident that UPR will create growth and value well beyond what Pennzoil can achieve on its own."
Union Pacific said the combined company would lead the industry in a number of performance measures, including drilling activity, production and cash flow.

Union Pacific said it would make a cash tender offer for 50.1 percent of Pennzoil's shares, starting Monday, followed by an exchange of shares for the remaining 49.9 percent. The Union Pacific shares will be worth $25 to $30 apiece depending on stock prices prior to the closing of the deal.
Union Pacific's stock lost $1 to $25.375, also on the NYSE.

Union Pacific Resources President George Lindahl said in a telephone interview that the company has held merger talks with Pennzoil for four months and decided to put the offer directly to shareholders. He said Union Pacific would borrow about $2 billion to finance the deal.
"Our financial strength means we do not have any plans to sell the Jiffy Lubes or motor oils division, which in any case account for only 10 percent of Pennzoil's business," he said.

Lindahl said Pennzoil had used cash from its U.S. business to fund its overseas development and noted that Pennzoil ranks 34th in terms of drilling in the United States, while Union Pacific ranks first.
"They have seven exploration rigs in the U.S.; we have 60. There are all kinds of possibilities and we will immediately ramp up their programme," Lindahl said.

Union Pacific's Messman sent a letter to Pennzoil Chairman James Pate, whom the company said in a statement has "repeatedly rebuffed UPR's efforts to have any serious discussion about a possible transaction."
"These two companies belong together," Messman said in the letter. Messman also said in the letter that Pate in 1995 proposed a merger with UPR, when it was a subsidiary of Union Pacific Corp.
Messman's letter also questioned Pate's view, contained in a May 8, 1997, letter to Messman, that a merger somehow no longer made sense, Union Pacific Resources said.

"We do not understand why you believed that two years ago, when Pennzoil faced particularly severe problems, it was in a better position than it is now to merge with UPR and form the premier independent E&P (energy and petroleum) company. In fact, we believe that today the benefits from a combination would come even more quickly," he wrote.
Union Pacific Resources said it sought a friendly merger but that its advances were repeatedly rebuffed.

"Your continued refusal to discuss the rationale or valuation of a transaction has left us with no choice but to present our offer directly to Pennzoil shareholders," Messman wrote. "While we are still prepared to discuss a friendly transaction, the UPR board of directors strongly supports pursuing a business combination now."
The deal requires approval by shareholders of both companies and regulators, Union Pacific Resources said.
